title: How to design a decision-grade pilot for agentic AI
summary:
Agentic AI changes the nature of a technology evaluation. When an AI system only generates an answer, a person reviews the output and decides whether to use it. An agent goes further: It gathers context, selects tools, makes decisions, and executes a sequence of actions across the software development lifecycle.

The central question for a pilot is therefore not whether the agent can produce an impressive result. It is: What evidence would be sufficient to authorize this agent to perform this workflow for this team?

A feature checklist or a collection of successful demos cannot answer that. Leaders need evidence about end-to-end task completion, reliability, control enforcement, level of human effort, operational risk, and economics. This article presents a framework for producing that evidence and turning an agentic AI pilot into a defensible decision.

Start with the decision, not the technology

A pilot should begin with the decision it is meant to support. "Evaluate agentic AI" is too broad. A usable decision names the workflow, the users, the proposed level of autonomy, the output the agent must produce, the acceptance criteria and metrics that define success, the quantified outcome the team expects, and the conditions under which it will proceed.

For example: Decide whether an AI agent can diagnose selected CI/CD pipeline failures and prepare a merge request with a proposed fix that passes the pipeline’s tests and is accepted by the developer, within defined repository permissions, while reducing total resolution effort by at least 25% against the current baseline.

This is more useful than "test an AI pipeline agent" because it fixes the output, the acceptance criteria, the control boundary, and the quantified outcome before anything runs.

Define what happens on success, too: a limited rollout with one team, expansion to more teams, and/or a higher level of autonomy. Without an agreed next decision, a pilot drifts into an open-ended experiment.

Define the proposed level of autonomy

Agentic AI is not simply "autonomous" or "not autonomous." The same agent can operate at different levels of authority. A useful model for a pilot has four levels:

  1. Recommend: The agent analyzes the situation and recommends an action.
  2. Prepare: The agent creates an artifact, such as a merge request, issue, or remediation plan, but does not apply it.
  3. Execute with approval: The agent acts only after an authorized person approves.
  4. Execute within boundaries: The agent acts on its own inside a predefined scope and escalates exceptions.

Test the level the team could realistically authorize. Evaluating only in recommendation mode says little about whether the agent can safely execute changes. Granting broad autonomy in an early evaluation adds risk without evidence.

Autonomy should be earned. A team can start with recommendations, move to prepared changes, and consider bounded execution only after the agent has shown sufficient reliability and control compliance.

Evaluate the workflow, not the response

Traditional model evaluation focuses on response quality. Agentic evaluation must focus on completing an end-to-end task.

Take an agent that helps resolve a failed pipeline. A plausible explanation is not the outcome. The workflow may require the agent to:

  • Identify the relevant job and logs, and separate the root cause from secondary symptoms.
  • Inspect the right configuration and code, and propose a valid correction without unrelated changes.
  • Create a reviewable artifact and trigger the correct validation steps.
  • Escalate when confidence or authorization is insufficient.

Define success at the workflow level: Did the agent reach the intended outcome correctly, within its authority, and with an acceptable amount of human effort? This keeps a convincing explanation from earning a pass when the agent does not reliably complete useful work.

Build an evaluation set from representative work

A decision-grade pilot needs an evaluation set that reflects the work the agent will actually meet, not scenarios chosen because they show the technology well. For each workflow, include:

  • Realistic tasks: common, well-understood tasks and complex but valid ones
  • Difficult inputs: ambiguous requests with missing or conflicting context, and unsafe or adversarial inputs where appropriate
  • Cases the agent must not complete on its own: expected failures, requests outside its authorization boundary, and high-impact actions that require human approval

Use sanitized examples from real workflows whenever possible. Generic exercises remove the dependencies, coding standards, policies, and ownership boundaries that make enterprise work difficult.

Add explicit acceptance criteria: a known correct diagnosis, tests that must pass, an expected security policy result, or a rubric completed by a subject matter expert. Without them, reviewers score how persuasive an output looks, which makes results hard to compare and easy to overestimate.

Measure a distribution, not the best run

Agentic systems behave differently when input, context, or execution state changes, so a single successful run says very little about reliability. AI output is variable and context-dependent, which is why evaluation has to look for patterns across representative scenarios rather than individual results. For agents there is one addition: Variability can affect actions, not only answers.

Run important scenarios several times, vary the relevant conditions, and measure:

  • Task outcomes: end-to-end success rate, reviewer acceptance rate, and failure rate by scenario type
  • Human involvement: intervention and escalation rate, and rework introduced by the agent
  • Controls and resilience: policy or authorization violations, plus latency and recovery from tool, context, or workflow failures

The goal is not to prove the agent always behaves identically. It is to understand the distribution of outcomes and decide whether it is acceptable for the proposed use. Where predictability is non-negotiable, as in release management, keep the agent out of the execution path. Let it prepare the artifact, such as a deployment script, and let the pipeline run that script, so the execution is deterministic and the agent’s variability is limited to what a reviewer can inspect beforehand. The same pattern works in operations: An agent can assess whether a rollback is needed, while the rollback itself runs as a tested script. In both cases the pilot measures the quality of what the agent prepares or recommends, which are the Prepare and Recommend levels.

Two cautions apply. First, aggregates hide risk: A 90% success rate is not strong if the other 10% includes unauthorized changes. Segment results by risk tier and failure type. Second, pilot samples are small, so report counts and uncertainty, not only percentages. Twenty successes in twenty runs does not demonstrate 99% reliability: At 95% confidence, the true failure rate could still be close to 14%. Eighteen out of twenty is consistent with a true success rate anywhere from roughly 70% to 97%. If a threshold matters, size the number of runs to it, or state plainly that the pilot cannot yet support the claim.

Set thresholds by risk, and treat controls as hard gates

Not every task needs the same reliability. A wrong explanation that a developer can ignore has a different impact from a wrong production change. Define risk tiers and apply different thresholds to each:

Risk tierExample actionEvaluation approach
LowExplain a pipeline errorMeasure usefulness and correctness; a human validates the response
MediumPrepare a merge requestRequire passing tests, scoped changes, and reviewer approval
HighMerge or deploy a changeRequire strict authorization, mandatory controls, reversibility, and a substantially higher reliability threshold



Some requirements are not thresholds at all. They are hard gates, and an agent cannot offset a failed gate with time saved elsewhere. Completing the task and respecting the control environment are inseparable: An agent that resolves a vulnerability by bypassing an approval rule has not completed the workflow. Typical must-pass gates include:

  • Identity and authorization: Every action is attributable to the agent and the initiating user, the agent works with least-privilege access, cannot reach tools outside its scope, and retrieves only the permitted context.
  • Policy and approval: Existing security and compliance policies still apply, and required human checkpoints cannot be bypassed.
  • Auditability and control: Reviewers can reconstruct what the agent did and why, high-impact changes can be undone, the team can stop or disable the agent, and failures, policy violations, and abnormal activity are visible.

GitLab's guidance on governing agentic AI treats role-based permissions, tool approval guardrails, and human review checkpoints as distinct control points for agent actions. A pilot should verify them with negative tests, not just confirm they exist on paper. Attempt actions outside the permitted scope, remove required context, trigger an approval boundary, and confirm that the agent stops, refuses, or escalates as designed.

Measure total effort and cost per successful task

Time saved by the agent is only one side of the equation. An agent can finish a task in minutes and leave a lengthy review. It can cut implementation time while raising the effort needed to understand the change. It can automate routine work and still produce occasional failures that need a senior specialist to diagnose.

Measure the whole workflow: preparing requests and context, reviewing output, correcting or reworking changes, handling escalations and failures, and the manual steps avoided. The useful metric is not minutes generated by the agent but total human effort per successfully completed task. Also record where human judgment remains essential. The aim is an effective operating model between people and agents, not necessarily removing people.

Apply the same logic to cost. A low-cost execution that frequently fails can cost more than a higher-cost one that completes the workflow correctly. Count model and platform consumption, tool and infrastructure usage, human review, rework and failed attempts, and monitoring and support overhead. Then compare with the current baseline:

  • Cost per successfully completed task
  • Total human effort and median time to completion per task, including the share of tasks that need specialist intervention
  • Rework or defect rate, and throughput under the same control requirements

The pilot does not need a perfect financial model. It needs to show whether the value stays credible once the costs a demonstration leaves out are included.

DimensionDecision questionExample evidenceThreshold type

Task successDoes the agent complete the end-to-end task correctly?Acceptance criteria, tests, expert reviewTarget
ReliabilityAre outcomes consistent across representative scenarios?Repeated runs, success and failure rates segmented by risk, with countsRisk-based target
Human effortDoes the agent reduce total effort after review and rework?Time study, intervention and escalation rateTarget
EconomicsIs the cost per successful task credible at expected scale?Consumption, operations, and support estimatesTarget
AuthorizationDoes the agent stay within its assigned permissions?Access and negative test resultsMust pass
GovernanceAre actions attributable, reviewable, and auditable?Approval records, audit trail, change historyMust pass
Safety and recoveryCan failures be detected, contained, and reversed?Failure injection, rollback, and disablement testsMust pass
AdoptionCan the intended users understand and operate the workflow?User observation, feedback, training needsTarget



Define thresholds before running the evaluation. Thresholds set after seeing results let teams adjust the definition of success to match what they observed. Record the evidence behind each result: a score without evidence is hard to defend and gives little guidance for rollout.

Worked example: A pipeline failure agent

The numbers below are illustrative, not benchmarks. They show how thresholds, segmentation, and gates combine into a decision.

A team wants an agent to diagnose failed pipelines and prepare a merge request with a fix, for developer approval (the Prepare level). They sanitize 30 real failures across three types and run each scenario three times, for 90 runs. Before running anything, they set the following thresholds:

  • Reviewer-accepted merge requests: at least 85% for configuration errors, 70% for flaky tests, and 85% for permission-related failures, where a wrong fix is costlier
  • Total human effort per resolved failure, including review and rework: at least 25% below the baseline median of 40 minutes
  • Hard gates: zero out-of-scope changes, zero bypassed approvals, and every merge request attributable to the agent and the initiating user
Failure typeRunsAcceptedRateThresholdResult
Configuration errors302790%85%Pass
Flaky tests302273%70%Pass
Permission-related301550%85%Fail



The median human effort was 29 minutes against 40, a 28% reduction. The gates held: no violations in 90 runs, and all 10 negative tests ended in a refusal or escalation. Zero violations in 90 runs supports a true violation rate below roughly 3% at 95% confidence, which is evidence but not proof.

The resulting decision is narrower than "the agent works." Authorize Prepare-level rollout for configuration errors and flaky tests. Keep permission-related failures at Recommend, fix the context the agent lacks, and repeat that tier. Do not authorize execution.

Governed agents across the software lifecycle

The gates above are platform-neutral, but GitLab Duo Agent Platform applies them across the whole software lifecycle instead of to a single tool. For a pilot, that means you can evaluate agents at several stages against one set of controls. Duo Agent Platform offers agents and flows at each stage:

  • Plan: Planner Agent plans, prioritizes, and tracks work, and Data Analyst Agent draws insight from development metrics.
  • Code: Developer Flow turns issues into merge requests, and Software Development Flow builds a multi-step plan before it acts.
  • Review: Code Review Flow automates review tasks and enforces coding standards, and GitLab Duo can also resolve review discussions and merge conflicts.
  • Build and deploy: Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow diagnoses and fixes failing pipelines, and Convert to GitLab CI/CD Flow migrates legacy pipelines.
  • Secure: SAST Vulnerability Resolution Flow generates fixes, the false positive detection flows filter static application security testing and secret detection findings, and Security Analyst Agent triages and analyzes vulnerabilities.

These capabilities sit at different points on the autonomy model. Developer Flow prepares a merge request for review, which is the Prepare level. Resolving merge conflicts or review discussions pushes commits, which is closer to execution, so a pilot should hold it to a stricter threshold.

The same guardrails apply across all of these stages:

  • Identity: Composite identity is the default for agent sessions. A flow acts through a service account combined with the user who triggered it, and permissions are the more restrictive of the two. Agentic Chat in the UI and IDE is the exception.
  • Approval: Agent tool governance (beta) sets each tool to Always Allow, Always Ask, or Always Deny at group or project level, and project rules can only be equal to or stricter than group rules. By default, write and delete tools ask for approval. Background flows have no user to ask, so their tools can only be allowed or denied, and a tool with no background rule is allowed. Set those rules explicitly, and confirm that enforcement for background flows, which is controlled by a feature flag, is on in your environment.
  • Audit: AI audit events (beta) give a per-session record, with actions attributed to the service account and the human who started the session recorded alongside. Storage is off by default and must be enabled. The AI Governance Dashboard (beta) adds group-level monitoring of agent sessions and developer exposure.
  • Data boundaries: Duo Agent Platform can run with self-hosted models on GitLab Self-Managed, for organizations that must control where model requests are processed.

Several of these controls are in beta, so treat them as part of what the pilot evaluates: confirm their status, enable them explicitly, and test them with the negative tests described earlier.

Turn the pilot into an authorization decision

A pilot should end with a decision about authority, scope, and operating conditions. Possible outcomes include:

  • Authorize a limited rollout to selected teams, at the evaluated autonomy level or for lower-risk tasks only.
  • Reduce the agent from execution to preparation or recommendation mode, or iterate on controls, context, or workflow design and repeat selected tests.
  • Stop, because value, reliability, risk, or economics are not acceptable.

Write the decision down. The record should state:

  • Scope: the workflows and task types covered and excluded, the authorized level of autonomy, and the systems, tools, and data the agent may access
  • Evidence and controls: the thresholds demonstrated, with run counts, the known limitations, and the controls and approval points that must stay active
  • Ownership: the workflow owner and escalation path, and the metrics monitored after rollout and the conditions that trigger suspension or reassessment

This ties pilot evidence to the authority actually delegated. It also stops a successful evaluation of one narrow workflow from being read as approval for broader autonomous use.

Start your own decision-grade pilot today

Evaluating agentic AI is an exercise in deciding how much authority a team is prepared to delegate, and under which conditions. The result of a decision-grade pilot should not be "the agent works." It should be a documented decision that states where the agent may act, what evidence supports that authority, which controls must stay in place, and how the team will know when to intervene. That is the standard for moving agentic AI from experimentation into responsible enterprise use.

title: The Pentagon wants to know who checks code when AI writes it
summary:
The Department of War now treats AI-generated code as unverified until it’s proven otherwise. DoW Instruction 8430.01, “Accelerated Mission Software,” took effect September 8, 2026, and is the department’s latest guidance on modernizing and managing software. If you build or buy software for the DoW, the instruction changes what’s required of you for every line AI writes. You have to review and test it to the same standard as human-written code, show where AI touched it, and keep it on systems the department has approved. Here’s what the instruction asks of your team, and how GitLab helps you address it.

What is DoW Instruction 8430.01?

Issued by DoW CIO Kirsten Davies, DoW Instruction 8430.01 applies to every DoW organization and to any acquisition program that includes software, regardless of cost. The instruction sets policy and procedures for modernizing and managing software, with an emphasis on delivering capabilities faster. It directs teams to automate testing and security scanning, reuse what already works, and produce evidence as software is built.

title: 10 questions to ask any software vendor about sovereignty
summary:
Sovereignty is moving from buzzword to buying criterion. The European Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) would set assurance levels for the cloud and AI services public authorities buy, defining where data should live and who can access it. Parts of it could reach private entities too.

GitLab submitted its own comment on CADA because we share the goal of strengthening Europe’s digital sovereignty and security. We believe this important work should prioritize customer control, portability, interoperability, provider diversity, and risk-based safeguards. You can also view GitLab's submission on the European Commission's Have Your Say portal.

But regulation is only one lever. Many vendor conversations still don’t address sovereignty with enough depth. If this is a priority for your organization, here are ten questions I’d put to any software vendor, GitLab included. Use them as a simple assessment to confirm if a vendor takes sovereignty seriously:

10 questions to ask your vendors

1. Which layers of the stack do you operate yourself?

This question gets at ownership and accountability. A cloud provider and a software vendor control different risks, and a good vendor can help its customers appropriately distinguish between the controls it operates from those it inherits from the infrastructure beneath it.

2. Can I choose where and how the software runs?

Look for a vendor that offers flexibility around how you handle your data and architecture. Sovereignty needs to vary by workload, and the architecture should be able to meet your requirements. For example, self-managed deployments let you run software on your own infrastructure, whether on-premises, in a private cloud, or in a hybrid setup, so your data stays within boundaries you define.

3. Can I choose the AI models I use, and change them later?

Frontier models change fast, and your vendor should not lock you to one. Look for platforms that are model agnostic and draw on a diverse set of models and hosts. That gives your business the flexibility to use the best model for each use case as new ones are released. Open-weight models can often run in your own environment while offering strong price-performance.

4. Does my data train anyone’s model?

Data is valuable for training AI models, so ask for an official written policy around model training and request it includes sub-processors too. Consider it a great sign if the vendor can confidently point to resources that affirm they do not train generative AI models on your data and restrict AI model sub-processors from using both model inputs and outputs for training.

5. What data leaves my region, and why?

Personal data of identifiable users remains subject to regional regulations, like GDPR, regardless of its origin. However, some data and operational signals need to cross boundaries to keep service secure and available. The right vendor offers local hosting and can otherwise explain what types of data cross borders and justify why.

6. Who can reach my data, and from where?

Ask which roles can reach your infrastructure and customer data, from which regions, and under what safeguards. A vendor that offers deployment options with customer-managed encryption keys and private network connectivity adds further control over that access.

7. How do you handle data and risk classifications?

Ask how the vendor classifies different data and what governance mechanisms and incident response activities are in place to handle policy violations and security incidents. A clear classification approach also feeds data protection impact assessments.

8. Which independent audits cover the service I am buying?

Attestations such as SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 let a vendor prove its own layer separately from the infrastructure provider’s assessment. Check that the report scope covers the application you will actually use.

9. Can you match controls to the sensitivity of each workload?

Regulated industries require finer-grain policy controls. Ask whether the vendor lets you set the level of assurance workload by workload. This approach helps your team tune controls to the sensitivity of its function and data so you have speed with control.

10. What does leaving your ecosystem look like?

Portability and interoperability are sovereignty features. Ask how the platform connects to the other tools and models you use and how you would export your projects and history. The format of data exports is important; exports often yield datasets that are complex, poorly structured, or intentionally obfuscated, making them difficult to process without technical restructuring. A vendor confident in its product welcomes easy exports and open integrations.

Sovereignty helps organizations embrace flexibility

No vendor will give perfect answers on all ten of these questions, and requirements will continue to evolve, but the architecture you choose should be poised to absorb changes resiliently.

Teams get the most from AI when they can decide what their organization controls and how. That’s why GitLab believes customers should be able to choose which models they use and where they run. Take these ten questions into your next vendor conversation and see which vendors take sovereignty as seriously as you do.

If you’d like to see how GitLab measures up (we do!), review how we handle customer data and infrastructure in our AI Transparency Center.

title: GitLab Orbit is GA: Higher agent accuracy, lower token cost
summary:
An agent’s true cost isn’t only the tokens it burns. It’s the review that calls your code “safe to merge” after seeing the diff, but without any context on the pipeline. We call that artificial confidence, not artificial intelligence. Agents guess because code is all they can see; they can’t see the merge request that last changed it, the pipeline that ran it, the vulnerability it carries, or the people who wrote and reviewed it.

Guessing is expensive. If you’ve tried running agents in a large monorepo, one with tens of thousands of files, you know how it goes: the agent iterates, pinging the backend again and again for the information it needs to complete the task. Every round trip costs more time and more tokens. Eventually the agent gives up.

The model isn’t the constraint. Context is.

That’s the constraint that GitLab Orbit removes. Now generally available, Orbit is the context graph for your software lifecycle: a live, queryable view of all your code, merge requests, work items, pipelines, vulnerabilities, and ownership, with every relationship continuously updated as you ship. Every agent and engineer can work from one connected view of the lifecycle. In GitLab testing, agents connected to Orbit needed up to 45x fewer retries and used 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model.

Grounded agents get answers right the first time

An agent like Claude Code, connected to GitLab Orbit through MCP, stops crawling files and instead asks the graph. The first response comes back with real callers, recent changes, and owners, so your follow-up prompts can refine the answer rather than correct it. The difference is measurable. Compare the Market, one of the UK’s largest price comparison platforms, tested four context approaches for an internal AI code reviewer across 79 real merge requests. The GitLab Orbit-grounded reviewer matched about 70% of expected inline comments; RAG managed about 58%, worse than no added context at all.

“GitLab Orbit gave us an AI code reviewer that actually understands our codebase, not just the diff in front of it. We tested it against RAG and a few other approaches across real merge requests, and the gap was clear. Better comment placement, better summaries of what actually changed.”

— Ryan Harvey, Head of AI Engineering, Compare the Market

Fewer retries means fewer tokens

A recent analysis from a leading research and advisory firm found that the cost of an undisciplined agent session is dominated by retransmitting context that didn’t change between turns. That token cost comes from how the agent is set up, not from the model itself.

GitLab Orbit changes that engineering. The agent gets one bounded answer from the graph instead of reloading everything that might matter. In GitLab testing, agents connected to Orbit used up to 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model: each turn carries less context, and fewer turns go to work that never ships. Because the graph is shared, that cost doesn’t repeat per agent. Duo agents, Claude Code, Codex, and your own tools all query the same graph, so the context you build for the first agent is already there for the second.

Questions you couldn’t answer before

Since GitLab Orbit entered beta in June, we’ve worked with design partners running it against real codebases, real incidents, and real merge requests. Their first win was almost always a question they couldn’t get answered before.

Here are a few questions design partners asked Orbit that they couldn’t answer before, and what came back:

Which production services are exposed to this vulnerability? A single query returns the services that include the component, the merge requests that introduced it, the environments it reached, and the teams that own each one. One design partner answered a security-coverage question across 34 million entities in seven minutes; through the API, the same question would have taken half a day. When a vulnerability lands, security has a complete remediation plan within the hour, not a partial list by the end of the day.

What breaks if I change this? Before a push, a developer or their agent can ask which services, jobs, and environments a change touches, across every project in the group, not just the one open in the editor. Review agents bring the same answer to the merge request, so a “safe to merge” comment reflects the whole system instead of the diff. Across 79 real merge requests, Compare the Market’s reviewer flagged more real issues in the right places than their RAG-based version. Problems get caught in review, before they become outages.

Why does this CI job keep failing, and where else? GitLab Orbit shows how often a job fails across every project that runs it, which projects have drifted from the shared CI configuration, and who owns them. What used to be a Slack thread asking three teams “has anyone seen this?” becomes one answer. A financial services company used this to trace a build-system outage to a CI job failing 50% of the time, a pattern nothing else had correlated.

What depends on the thing we’re about to migrate? Every dependent service, job, environment, and owner comes back in one result. One design partner finished a multi-repository upgrade by asking the question directly: which projects are still on the old version? The last stragglers could be surfaced in one query with no spreadsheet or repo-by-repo audit to contend with.

Not every context graph can answer them

Context graphs are becoming a category, and most of them stop at code. GitLab connects the code change to the pipeline, the deployment, the vulnerability, and the owner, with your permissions intact. This means your team and agents can:

  • Start with a graph that already exists. GitLab Orbit draws on the data you already have in GitLab, which means there is no connector to configure, no ETL pipeline to maintain, and no second system of record to keep in sync. Enable it for a group and the graph is ready. A graph assembled from the outside takes months of integration work before it answers its first question. Orbit is also built to extend to non-GitLab data sources.
  • Index the whole lifecycle. GitLab is the system of record for the entire software development lifecycle, and GitLab Orbit connects it into one graph. Code indexes stop at the code. Work graphs stop at the ticket.
  • Keep your permissions without rebuilding them. GitLab Orbit mirrors nested groups, roles, and security-domain access. A graph that lives outside GitLab has to rebuild all of that and keep it in sync.
  • Give every agent and every engineer the same graph. Duo agents, Claude Code, Codex, custom tools, and the Data Explorer all query the same graph the same way. You invest in context once and every agent you add after that is cheaper than the last.

Bring the agents you already use

GitLab Orbit doesn’t ask you to change how your team works. The agents and tools you already run connect to one graph:

  • Agents on GitLab Duo Agent Platform query GitLab Orbit natively, with nothing to configure.
  • Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, and any other MCP-compatible agent connect through MCP or the GitLab CLI:
glab auth login
glab orbit setup
  • Custom agents and internal tooling connect through REST.
  • Engineers query the same graph through the Data Explorer.

Every path asks the same graph the same way, and the graph keeps up. GitLab Orbit indexes every push, merge, and deploy as it happens, so agents reason from the lifecycle in its most current state; at GitLab’s scale, that’s more than 1.5 million projects and 8TB of graph data in under 2 hours. Indexing runs as its own service beside GitLab, so however hard your agents use Orbit, GitLab itself never slows down.

Pricing: One shared query pool for your whole organization

GitLab Orbit is sold as query packs that form one shared pool sized for your organization. Everyone in your GitLab org draws from it, humans and agents alike, so usage flows between occasional users, power users, and the agents working on their behalf. Nobody requests access or gets assigned a seat. A query is one request to the Orbit graph, whether it comes from an agent (such as Duo Agent Platform, Claude Code, or Cursor), an experience built into GitLab, or the API.

Each query pack is $30 in GitLab Credits per user per month and adds 1,000 queries to your organization’s shared pool; usage beyond the pool is billed at 33 queries per GitLab Credit, about $0.03 per query. Promotional pricing is available this quarter for early customers. Contact your GitLab account team to learn more and size the right number of query packs for your organization.

Get started with GitLab Orbit

GitLab Orbit is now generally available for Premium and Ultimate customers, starting with GitLab.com today and reaching Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated over the coming weeks. Customers can try it free for 30 days through their GitLab account team. If you’re brand new to GitLab, talk to our sales team about getting started with a GitLab paid plan, and we can help you add an Orbit trial as part of it.

Check out our documentation to help you get started.

title: GitLab Orbit: Find vulnerability blast radius without the manual hunt
summary:
A critical vulnerability needs a fix and a map. The fix is usually fast. Finding where the vulnerable component lives, who owns it, and whether it's exposed to the Internet is what costs you time. Most security teams piece that answer together from scanner reports, spreadsheets, and a Slack thread asking who owns a service nobody recognizes, and you stay exposed for every hour that takes.

GitLab Orbit, now generally available, replaces this manual work with a single query. Orbit connects code, merge requests, pipelines, security findings, and ownership in one graph that stays current as your teams ship. Ask which projects are affected and who owns them, and you get an answer in minutes. Agents answer from the graph instead of crawling repositories and stitching together API calls, so they need fewer retries and fewer tokens to get there.

Why scanners alone can't answer the question

PHP2Shell, the set of critical PHP flaws disclosed last week, illustrates the problem. PHP is usually installed as a system package, compiled from source, or baked into a container image, not managed as an application dependency. Vulnerable versions can sit on web servers, in container images, in old CI jobs, or in internal tools nobody remembers building. The fix was a version upgrade. Finding every affected installation took time.

Security tools provide different views of the environment. Dependency scanning identifies vulnerable application dependencies. Container scanning detects vulnerabilities in operating system packages, language dependencies, and other software components. Code search helps locate where images and configurations are referenced. But identifying a vulnerability is only part of the job. Teams still need to know which services are affected, who owns them, which pipelines build and deploy them, and where to apply the fix. That information is often spread across multiple systems.

That leaves your team to connect the dots, each holding a different piece. Your security engineer can assess the severity but may not see every affected system. Your platform engineer owns the base images and CI templates that hundreds of projects depend on, but can't see every project that uses them. Your developers get pulled off their roadmap to search repositories for a component they may not know they own. Your CISO has to tell leadership whether the company is exposed before anyone has a full list.

An attacker only needs to find one vulnerable system. You need to find all of them. Exploiting a vulnerability is now the most common way breaches begin, at 31% in Verizon's 2026 report, and the same report found attackers using generative AI at several stages of an attack. The map needs to exist before the advisory lands.

A first-party graph of your entire SDLC

Orbit draws on the data GitLab already runs on: your merge requests, pipelines, deployments, and vulnerabilities. A CVE in Orbit's graph connects directly to the services, pipelines, environments, and teams it touches. Because the graph is first-party, there's no second system to keep in sync and no new instrumentation to stand up.

Without Orbit, an agent or analyst can usually find the vulnerable code but not the full exposure. Someone assembles that picture by hand, tool by tool, and the gaps show up as the long tail of services nobody checked. With Orbit, one query maps the CVE to the services, pipelines, environments, and owners that depend on it, and the output is a scoped, prioritized list your security team can act on.

Agents without Orbit hit the same wall: they can't see the whole system, so they guess. In GitLab's testing on the same tasks with the same model, agents running through Orbit were up to 11 times faster, used up to 4.5 times fewer tokens, and needed up to 45 times fewer retries. During an incident, faster answers arrive while the team is still triaging, lower token use keeps queries across a large group from becoming a cost problem, and fewer retries mean your team can act on the first answer instead of re-running the question.

Watch the demo to learn how GitLab Orbit can help you understand your exposure:

One graph that connects a CVE to its owner

Blast radius is how far a vulnerability reaches: which projects contain the flawed component, how it got there, who owns those projects, and what changed recently. GitLab already holds most of those facts in separate places, and Orbit connects them. Turn it on for a top-level group, and Orbit indexes projects, merge requests, pipelines, work items, security findings, and source code into one graph of how they relate.

From there, you ask in plain language instead of correlating systems by hand: which projects use this library, which merge requests brought it in, and who owns each project? An agent traverses the graph and answers from indexed project data, and you can audit the graph queries behind each answer.

Access follows the roles you've already set, so people and agents see only what they're permitted to see. GitLab's built-in agents, including the Security Analyst Agent, use Orbit directly, and external agents such as Claude Code and Codex reach the same graph over MCP.

Contain your exposure quickly

After PHP2Shell, leadership's first question is whether you're exposed. Without a map, your answer is "we're checking." With Orbit, your answer is a list: these projects contain PHP, these teams own them, and these pipelines build them.

The first hour with Orbit looks like this:

  1. Find every PHP project. In GitLab Duo Agentic Chat, ask: “Use Orbit to map the blast radius of PHP in this group. List every project that contains PHP code, grouped by subgroup, with owners.”
  2. Confirm the base image and version. Use exact code search at the top-level group with regular expression mode on. Run lang:Dockerfile ^FROM.*php to find container base images, and file:composer\.json$ to find Composer projects with no Dockerfile. Compare each FROM tag with the fixed versions.
  3. Find open findings. Once scans have run, ask Agentic Chat to collect every container scanning finding for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 across the group from the vulnerability report. This requires Ultimate and the Security Manager role.
  4. Check against what’s running. Orbit and code search cover what your repositories declare on the default branch. Compare that list with your runtime inventory from configuration management or cloud tooling, starting with internet-facing services, since PHP can also run on hand-built servers outside any repository.

The PHP2Shell remediation guide covers fixed versions and how to check for compromise. Teams on GitLab Self-Managed or GitLab Dedicated can start with the guide's advanced search and repository languages API steps until Orbit reaches their instance.

Run the same check for any shared component

The steps above work beyond PHP. When a widely used library ships a security fix, a package you depend on is flagged as malicious, a CI template many projects inherit needs a change, or an internal SDK ships a breaking security upgrade, you start with the same question: what depends on it, and who owns it? Orbit answers from the same graph each time, so your team starts from a list instead of a search.

Map your blast radius before the next disclosure

GitLab Orbit is now generally available for Premium and Ultimate customers, starting with GitLab.com today and reaching Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated over the coming weeks. Customers can try it free for 30 days through their GitLab account team. If you're new to GitLab, talk to our team about getting started with a paid plan, and we can add an Orbit trial as part of it.

Check out the documentation to get started. For a broader view of your security posture, request your GitLab Security Standard assessment to see how blast radius mapping fits into the rest of your security program. If your teams run PHP, start with the PHP2Shell remediation guide and upgrade now.
